vignette:
Mihai had been 76 for only a few months when he finally agreed that he could no longer manage on his own. He was a widowed cashier in a small grocery store on the edge of a Midwestern city, a place where his routine had once been simple and steady: early shift, the same customers, the same walk from the bus stop. Long before that, as a young man in a European war zone, he had been caught in a street bombardment while crossing to fetch bread for his family. He remembered the blast mostly as fragments of image: a wall splitting open, dust lifting in a white cloud, a woman's shoe in the road, his own hands pressed to the pavement. Even now, when he spoke of it, he often drifted into a flat, distant tone, saying it was "like it happened to someone else," yet at other moments the scene arrived with terrifying force, and he was back in the street with the sound and light returning all at once. The memory was not a story he could tell in sequence; it came as pictures, as flashes, and those flashes carried the feeling that the danger was immediate.

After the war, Mihai had tried to build a life by keeping quiet and staying useful, but over the years he came to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe. The bombardment had convinced him that danger could appear without warning, and that conviction made the images of the event more gripping whenever they surfaced. The more he told himself that the world had changed forever, the more the memory of that street seemed to sharpen around him, returning not as something past but as proof that he had been caught once and could be caught again. That belief kept drawing him back into the scene, colouring it with the thought that he should have known better and making it harder to let the image fade. Once they did, he found himself scanning his surroundings for signs that trouble was near. When the world felt that threatening, the only sensible answer in Mihai's mind was to narrow it as much as he could, which is why he kept changing routes, sitting near exits, and avoiding situations that might leave him trapped. Those precautions gave him brief relief, but they also made the danger feel even more real, as if his own caution were confirming what he feared. In the store he watched customers' hands, their faces, the way they stood too close to the counter. On the bus he chose a seat near the door and kept one eye on the other passengers. At night he lay awake because he felt he had to stay alert, as if sleep were a careless act that might let something happen. What frightened him most was not only what had happened then, but what the memory seemed to prove now: that the world remained dangerous and that he was no longer the capable man he had once been. Living with that level of danger all the time slowly hardened into a belief that this was simply who he was now - someone permanently altered, less steady, less able to protect himself. The threat he felt every day quietly became evidence for that conclusion.

Those images also changed the way he moved through daily life. When the pictures came back, he immediately began rearranging his days around them: leaving the store before the afternoon rush, choosing seats where he could see the door, and keeping himself busy so there was no quiet in which the scene might take hold. For Mihai, those habits were not separate from the memory but a way of pushing it down whenever it threatened to rise. Mihai stopped driving after an episode at a traffic light when the sight of a sudden brake light and a distant bang from construction work pulled him back into the blast scene so sharply that he had to grip the wheel and wait for it to pass. Since then he avoided being a passenger as well, preferring to walk longer distances or decline invitations rather than risk the enclosed space of a car. He had come to think that staying away from driving was the only sensible choice, because once the pictures arrived he could not trust himself to remain steady. When the memories surged, he felt on guard all over again, and that tension fed his sense that he must watch everyone closely for possible harm. The more he arranged his life around staying alert, the more he seemed to confirm to himself that danger was everywhere.

Mihai's attempts to make sense of the trauma also kept it close. Each time he pulled the event apart looking for a reason, he came away with the same harsh conclusion that something was wrong with him, and that thought made the memory easier to fall back into. He would start with one question and end back at the bombardment, convinced that the scene said something permanent about who he had become. He spent long evenings asking why such a thing had happened to him, turning the event over in his mind in search of an explanation or a reason, but the questions only deepened his conviction that life had betrayed him. He said he had lost his faith in people and in any higher power that might have protected the innocent, and when he thought about the bombardment in that way the memory became more than a recollection; it became evidence that no one could be trusted and that he himself was no longer capable of the sort of self-reliance that had once defined him. He had once been the man who worked, drove, made decisions, and kept his family safe. Now he felt diminished by his own startle response and by the need to check exits, sit with his back to the wall, and keep watch on the faces around him.

Over time, Mihai's efforts to push away any feeling that seemed too warm or hopeful also narrowed his world. Because he had spent so much energy keeping the war out of mind, the memories never felt settled; they broke through more abruptly when they did appear, as if being held at a distance had kept them raw. He noticed that the less he allowed himself to think or speak about it, the more easily the scene returned with its dust, noise, and panic intact. He no longer allowed himself to enjoy an afternoon with a neighbor or the small pleasure of a kind conversation at the register, because positive feelings seemed unsafe to him, as if lowering his guard might invite another blow. That restraint left him emotionally cut off and more certain that he was living in a hostile world. He missed his wife deeply, yet even grief felt risky because it could open the door to the images and the numbness that followed them. Sometimes he could recall the bombing and feel nothing at all, as though it had happened to a stranger; other times the street, the dust, and the sense of imminent death would come back so vividly that he felt he was in it again. Each time, the memory made him more watchful, more convinced that people could not be trusted, and more committed to keeping himself away from anything that might stir it up.

By the time he sought help, Mihai was exhausted by this narrowed life. He still went to work, but he moved through the grocery store as if through a perimeter he had to defend, and the bus ride there had become a daily ordeal. He came because the sleeplessness and constant vigilance were wearing him down, and because he feared that if he kept living this way he would disappear into fear before he truly became unable to do anything at all. What he hoped for, though he said it quietly, was not to forget the war but to be able to remember it without feeling hunted by it, and to believe again-at least a little-that he might still be safe among other people.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs about safety, but it does not clearly state that these negative appraisals drive or intensify the traumatic memory within the same paragraph.
The memory is described as triggering vigilance and avoidance, but no paragraph explicitly says the memory leads to maladaptive strategies such as avoidance or safety behaviors.

The vignette says the memory makes him more watchful and convinced people cannot be trusted, but it does not explicitly present the memory as causing negative appraisals in the required causal direction within a paragraph.
The vignette describes threat and hypervigilance, but it does not explicitly state that perceived threat leads to maladaptive strategies like avoidance or checking behaviors in the same paragraph.
Although he feels unsafe and mistrustful, no paragraph explicitly shows threat producing negative appraisals as a causal step.
The vignette states that coping efforts keep the trauma close or confirm danger, but it does not explicitly show maladaptive strategies causing the traumatic memory to recur or intensify.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette shows negative beliefs about safety, but it does not clearly state that these negative appraisals drive or intensify the traumatic memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The memory is described as triggering vigilance and avoidance, but no paragraph explicitly says the memory leads to maladaptive strategies such as avoidance or safety behaviors.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette says the memory makes him more watchful and convinced people cannot be trusted, but it does not explicitly present the memory as causing negative appraisals in the required causal direction within a paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes threat and hypervigilance, but it does not explicitly state that perceived threat leads to maladaptive strategies like avoidance or checking behaviors in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Although he feels unsafe and mistrustful, no paragraph explicitly shows threat producing negative appraisals as a causal step.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette states that coping efforts keep the trauma close or confirm danger, but it does not explicitly show maladaptive strategies causing the traumatic memory to recur or intensify.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
